description: Software architecture fundamentals (characteristics, modularity, styles, ADRs) merged with Domain-Driven Design strategic and tactical patterns. For a platform/enterprise architect who designs and reviews systems.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::01 Architectural Thinking
notes.text: Richards & Ford define software architecture by four dimensions: {{c1::structure}} (the style), {{c2::architecture characteristics}} (the "-ilities"), {{c3::architecture decisions}} (hard rules) and {{c4::design principles}} (guidelines).

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::01 Architectural Thinking
notes.back: “Everything in software architecture is a tradeoff.”
notes.extra: Corollary: if you think you found something that isn't a tradeoff, you haven't identified the tradeoff yet. Hence: "no right or wrong answers, only expensive ones."

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::01 Architectural Thinking
notes.back: “Why is more important than how.”
notes.extra: The rationale outlives the implementation; this is why ADRs record context and consequences.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::01 Architectural Thinking
notes.back: A decision is a hard rule that must be followed; a principle is a guideline that leaves implementation latitude.
notes.extra:
Decision: "all calls go through the business layer."
Principle: "prefer async messaging where practical."

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::01 Architectural Thinking
notes.front: Why should an architect favour technical breadth over depth?
notes.back: Decisions require knowing that many options exist (a large "know you don't know" zone); deep expertise in one stack narrows the options you can weigh.
notes.analogy: A GP who knows which specialist to call beats a brilliant specialist who sees every problem through one organ.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::01 Architectural Thinking
notes.back: An architect who reverts to one past bad experience as a worst-case worry on every decision, instead of assessing risk realistically per situation.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::01 Architectural Thinking
notes.front: Is the architecture/design boundary a line? How do you tell them apart?
notes.back: A spectrum: strategic, hard-to-change, high-effort decisions lean architectural; tactical, easy-to-change ones lean design.
notes.extra: Implication: architects and developers collaborate continuously rather than throwing decisions over the wall.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::01 Architectural Thinking
notes.back: Architecture is refined incrementally as understanding grows, with automated fitness functions guarding the important characteristics as it changes.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::02 Architecture Characteristics
notes.text: Something is an architecture characteristic if it (1) specifies a {{c1::non-domain}} design consideration, (2) influences a {{c2::structural}} aspect of the design, and (3) is {{c3::critical or important}} to the application's success.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::02 Architecture Characteristics
notes.text: Architecture characteristic categories: {{c1::operational}} (availability, performance, scalability), {{c2::structural}} (modularity, maintainability, extensibility), {{c3::cross-cutting}} (security, accessibility, privacy).

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::02 Architecture Characteristics
notes.back: Implicit: rarely written in requirements but almost always needed (availability, security). Explicit: stated directly in the requirements.
notes.extra: Pitfall: implicit ones get missed; ask about them in every requirements conversation.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::02 Architecture Characteristics
notes.front: Why deliberately limit the number of architecture characteristics you optimise for?
notes.back: Each one adds complexity and many conflict; chasing all yields a generic, over-engineered design. Aim for the least worst architecture, not the best.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::02 Architecture Characteristics
notes.front: Why can't you maximise all architecture characteristics? Give an example.
notes.back: Improving one often degrades another, so you balance. E.g. more security checks and encryption usually cost performance.
notes.analogy: Like a car: tuning for top speed costs fuel economy and comfort.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::02 Architecture Characteristics
notes.text: Architecture characteristics can be measured as {{c1::operational}} measures (response time, throughput), {{c2::structural}} measures (cyclomatic complexity, coupling) and {{c3::process}} measures (deployability, testability).

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::02 Architecture Characteristics
notes.back: An objective, automatable check of whether the architecture still meets a desired characteristic, e.g. a test that fails on forbidden layer dependencies.
notes.analogy: A unit test for an architecture quality instead of for a function.
notes.extra: Runs in CI, turning governance from review meetings into continuous feedback.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::03 Modularity & Coupling
notes.back: How strongly the parts of a module belong together (related, focused responsibilities). High cohesion is desirable.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::03 Modularity & Coupling
notes.back: Afferent (Ca): incoming, how many components depend on this one. Efferent (Ce): outgoing, how many it depends on.
notes.analogy: Mnemonic: Afferent = Arrives, Efferent = Exits.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::03 Modularity & Coupling
notes.front: Formula for instability \(I\), and what does a high value mean?
notes.back: \(I = \frac{C_e}{C_e + C_a}\). Near 1: depends on much, little depends on it, so it's easy (and likely) to change.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::03 Modularity & Coupling
notes.front: Formula for distance from the main sequence \(D\)?
notes.back: \(D = |A + I - 1|\), where \(A\) = abstractness (abstract / total elements). Near 0 = healthy balance.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::03 Modularity & Coupling
notes.back: Pain: highly concrete and stable (much depends on it), so it's rigid and hard to change. Uselessness: highly abstract and unstable, abstractions nobody uses.
notes.extra: Healthy components sit near the main sequence line between them.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::03 Modularity & Coupling
notes.back: Two components are connascent if changing one requires changing the other to keep the system correct.
notes.analogy: Like a three-legged race: if one runner changes stride, the other must too.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::03 Modularity & Coupling
notes.text: Static connascence (visible in source): connascence of {{c1::Name}}, {{c2::Type}}, {{c3::Meaning}} (convention, e.g. magic values), {{c4::Position}} (argument order) and {{c5::Algorithm}} (e.g. same hash on both sides).

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::03 Modularity & Coupling
notes.text: Dynamic connascence (visible only at runtime): connascence of {{c1::Execution}} (order), {{c2::Timing}}, {{c3::Values}} (values that must change together) and {{c4::Identity}} (same entity referenced).

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::03 Modularity & Coupling
notes.front: Why is dynamic connascence generally worse than static?
notes.back: Static tools and compilers can't detect it, so breakages surface only at runtime.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::03 Modularity & Coupling
notes.text: Connascence is evaluated by {{c1::strength}} (how hard to refactor), {{c2::locality}} (how close the elements are) and {{c3::degree}} (how many elements are affected).
notes.extra: Rule: the further apart two elements are, the weaker the connascence between them should be.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::03 Modularity & Coupling
notes.front: What is a component in architecture terms?
notes.back: The main modular building block (library, package, service, layer); the lowest level an architect usually manipulates directly.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::03 Modularity & Coupling
notes.back: An independently deployable unit with high functional cohesion and synchronous connascence inside it. A monolith is one quantum; microservices are many.
notes.analogy: A fleet vs one big ship: each microservice can sail (deploy) on its own; a monolith leaves port all at once.
notes.extra: Characteristics can differ per quantum, which is a key reason to split a system.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::03 Modularity & Coupling
notes.back: Static: how parts are wired (dependencies, contracts, infrastructure needed to run). Dynamic: how parts communicate at runtime (sync vs async).

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.front: Monolithic vs distributed architecture styles: which are which?
notes.back: Monolithic (one deployment unit): layered, pipeline, microkernel. Distributed: service-based, event-driven, space-based, SOA, microservices.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.front: Which characteristics push you from a monolith to a distributed style, and at what price?
notes.back: Scalability/elasticity, fault isolation, independent deployability, evolvability. Price: cost, operational complexity, network latency.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.text: Fallacies of distributed computing: the network is {{c1::reliable}}; latency is {{c2::zero}}; bandwidth is {{c3::infinite}}; the network is {{c4::secure}}; topology {{c5::never changes}}; there is {{c6::one administrator}}; transport cost is {{c7::zero}}; the network is {{c8::homogeneous}}.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: No discernible architecture: tangled, highly coupled code, usually from unmanaged organic growth.
notes.analogy: A house extended room by room with no plan, where every pipe runs through every wall.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: Horizontal layers (presentation → business → persistence → database), each usually closed.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: A closed layer must be passed through by requests going down; an open layer may be bypassed.
notes.extra: Closed layers give layers of isolation: a change in one layer doesn't ripple into the others.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: Requests pass through layers that do nothing but forward them, adding overhead without value.
notes.analogy: A chain of managers who just forward the email.
notes.extra: Rule of thumb: ~20% pass-through is fine; if most requests are, consider opening layers or another style.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.front: When is the layered style a sensible choice?
notes.back: Small/simple apps, tight budgets, or as a starting point when the right style is unclear: it's simple, cheap and familiar.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: Monolithic: poor scalability, elasticity, fault tolerance and deployability; prone to the sinkhole antipattern.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: Self-contained, stateless filters connected by one-way pipes.
notes.analogy: An assembly line: each station does one job and passes the part on.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.text: Pipeline filter types: {{c1::producer}} (source), {{c2::transformer}} (changes data), {{c3::tester}} (filters/branches on a condition), {{c4::consumer}} (sink).

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: A minimal core system plus independent plug-in components, found via a registry and connected by contracts.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: Product-type software where volatile or customer-specific logic can be isolated in plug-ins: IDEs, browsers, rules/claims engines.
notes.analogy: A browser and its extensions.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: A UI calling a few (≈4–12) coarse-grained, separately deployed domain services, usually over a shared database.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.front: Why is service-based called the most pragmatic distributed style?
notes.back: It gets much of microservices' benefit (deployability, fault isolation, evolvability) with far less complexity, since services are few and share a database.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: Service-based: few coarse domain services, usually one shared DB. Microservices: many fine-grained services, each owning its data.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: Decoupled event processors reacting to events asynchronously, in a broker or mediator topology.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: Broker: no coordinator; processors react and emit events. Decoupled and fast, but workflow and errors are hard. Mediator: a central mediator orchestrates steps. Better error handling, more coupling.
notes.analogy: Broker = a relay of gossip; mediator = a conductor cueing each section.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: Low simplicity and testability, complex error handling, non-deterministic flows and eventual consistency.
notes.extra: Strengths: performance, scalability, elasticity, fault tolerance, responsiveness.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: Processing units with replicated in-memory data grids, virtualized middleware, and async data pumps to the database.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.front: How does space-based architecture remove the database bottleneck?
notes.back: Processing units work on replicated in-memory data; the database is updated asynchronously via data pumps and writers, off the request path.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: High, spiky, unpredictable load needing extreme elasticity (ticketing, auctions, flash sales), accepting complexity and cost.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: A hierarchical service taxonomy (business, enterprise, application, infrastructure services) mediated by a central orchestration engine / ESB.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.front: Why did orchestration-driven SOA fall out of favour?
notes.back: Maximising reuse plus central ESB mediation coupled everything: one change rippled widely, killing evolvability and deployability.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: Fine-grained, single-purpose services, each owning its data, deployed independently, often behind an API gateway.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.front: Why do microservices map one service per bounded context?
notes.back: Each service owns one model and its data, so there's no shared-schema coupling and each can change and deploy independently.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.front: Why do microservices prefer duplication over coupling?
notes.back: Shared code or data couples deployments; duplicating small things keeps services independently changeable. The opposite of SOA's reuse goal.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.front: Why do microservices score poorly on performance?
notes.back: Each request crosses many network hops, with serialization and per-call security checks, and may need distributed transactions.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.front: Why is simplicity rated high for layered/microkernel but low for microservices?
notes.back: Monoliths have no network, no distributed data and few deployment units; microservices add all of these plus heavy operational tooling.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: Choreography: services react to events, no coordinator. Better decoupling. Orchestration: a coordinator drives the workflow. Easier error handling, more coupling.
notes.analogy: Choreography = dancers who know their cues; orchestration = musicians following a conductor.
notes.extra: Same tradeoff as event-driven broker vs mediator.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.front: Sidecar and service mesh: what problem do they solve in microservices?
notes.back: Cross-cutting operational concerns (telemetry, discovery, mTLS) live in a sidecar beside each service; together the sidecars form a mesh. Business code stays free of them.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::04 Architecture Styles
notes.back: Keeps data consistent across services without distributed ACID transactions: a sequence of local transactions, with compensating transactions to undo work on failure.
notes.analogy: Booking a trip: if the hotel fails, you cancel the flight you already booked.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::05 Decisions, Risk & Communication
notes.back: A short document recording one architecture decision, preserving the "why" (Second Law) as a durable, reviewable history.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::05 Decisions, Risk & Communication
notes.extra: Status values: proposed, accepted, superseded (link to the replacing ADR, never delete).

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::05 Decisions, Risk & Communication
notes.analogy: Like zooming a map from country to city to street to building.
notes.extra: Use consistent notation, a legend and labelled lines.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::05 Decisions, Risk & Communication
notes.back: Rate each risk by likelihood × impact (low/medium/high, 1–3); the product ranks which risks need attention first.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::05 Decisions, Risk & Communication
notes.front: Risk storming: why identify risks individually first?
notes.back: Participants mark risks on the diagram independently, then converge, so the group finds risks one architect would miss without groupthink.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::06 DDD Model & Language
notes.front: Domain model in DDD: what is it, and what is it not?
notes.back: A selective, agreed abstraction of domain knowledge, expressed in code, language and diagrams together. Not a diagram, not a copy of reality.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::06 DDD Model & Language
notes.back: Developers and domain experts iteratively distil domain information into a sharp model by testing it against concrete scenarios. Modeling is ongoing learning.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::06 DDD Model & Language
notes.back: One shared language built on the domain model, used by developers and domain experts in speech, diagrams and code, so nothing needs translating.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::06 DDD Model & Language
notes.front: In DDD, what does it signal when a domain term is awkward to use in code?
notes.back: A flaw or missing concept in the model: refine the model and language together, don't paper over it.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::06 DDD Model & Language
notes.back: The code is a direct expression of the model, so changing one changes the other. No separate analysis model that drifts away.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::06 DDD Model & Language
notes.front: Hands-On Modelers: why must modelers touch the code?
notes.back: Splitting modeling from implementation breaks the feedback loop; models made by non-coders don't survive contact with the code.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::06 DDD Model & Language
notes.back: Promote a concept hidden in comments, procedures or tangled conditionals into an explicit model object. Expert language and design awkwardness reveal them.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::06 DDD Model & Language
notes.back: A sudden leap to a much deeper model after sustained incremental refactoring toward insight. It can't be scheduled, only enabled.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::06 DDD Model & Language
notes.front: Why does DDD isolate the domain layer (UI / Application / Domain / Infrastructure)?
notes.back: Without isolation, business logic smears across UI and persistence code and becomes invisible and untestable.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::06 DDD Model & Language
notes.back: Application: thin, coordinates tasks and directs domain objects, no business rules. Domain: the business concepts, rules and state.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::06 DDD Model & Language
notes.front: Smart UI anti-pattern: when is it actually fine?
notes.back: All logic in the UI (event handlers, form procedures). Fine for simple apps needing quick delivery; it gives up any domain model, so it can't grow.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::07 DDD Tactical Building Blocks
notes.back: An object defined by a continuous identity over time, not by its attributes. All attributes may change, it stays the same thing.
notes.analogy: A person: name and address change, the passport number tracks the same human.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::07 DDD Tactical Building Blocks
notes.back: An object defined only by its attributes, with no identity (Money, Address). Immutable, interchangeable and freely shareable.
notes.analogy: A €10 note: you don't care which one you get, only its value.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::07 DDD Tactical Building Blocks
notes.front: Entity or Value Object: how do you decide?
notes.back: Ask: do we need to track which one this is over time? Yes → Entity. Only the values matter → Value Object (the default).

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::07 DDD Tactical Building Blocks
notes.front: DDD Domain Service: when do you use one?
notes.back: For a stateless domain operation that doesn't belong to any one Entity or Value Object (e.g. transfer funds between accounts). Named as a verb.
notes.extra: Pitfall: overuse strips behaviour out of entities, giving an anemic model.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::07 DDD Tactical Building Blocks
notes.front: DDD Module: how should modules be cut?
notes.back: By cohesive domain concepts, named in the Ubiquitous Language, not by technical type ("controllers", "utils").

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::07 DDD Tactical Building Blocks
notes.back: A cluster of Entities and Value Objects treated as one unit for data changes: the consistency boundary that enforces its invariants.
notes.analogy: An order with its order lines: you change lines only through the order, which keeps the total valid.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::07 DDD Tactical Building Blocks
notes.back: Outsiders may hold references only to the root; the root controls all access to internal members and guarantees the invariants.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::07 DDD Tactical Building Blocks
notes.front: Why should a transaction not span multiple aggregates?
notes.back: Invariants are kept inside one aggregate, so one local transaction can enforce them; rules across aggregates can be eventually consistent.
notes.analogy: Keep the rules that must always hold inside one vault, so one lock protects them.
notes.extra: Large multi-aggregate transactions cause lock contention and don't survive distribution.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::07 DDD Tactical Building Blocks
notes.back: To encapsulate complex creation of objects/aggregates so they are born in a valid state with all invariants met.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::07 DDD Tactical Building Blocks
notes.back: An abstraction giving the illusion of an in-memory collection of aggregate roots, hiding persistence and queries. One per aggregate root.
notes.analogy: A library desk: you ask for a book by title; you don't care where the stacks are.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::07 DDD Tactical Building Blocks
notes.back: Factory creates new objects; Repository finds and stores existing ones (it may use a factory to reconstitute them).

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::07 DDD Tactical Building Blocks
notes.back: A predicate object stating a business rule ("does this candidate satisfy X?"), used for validation, selection and build-to-order; combinable with and/or/not.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::08 DDD Supple Design
notes.back: Name classes and operations after their effect and purpose, not their mechanism. If you must read the implementation to use it, it fails.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::08 DDD Supple Design
notes.front: Side-Effect-Free Functions: why push logic into them?
notes.back: Functions that return results without changing state are safe to combine and test; keep state-changing commands small and separate (cf. CQS).

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::08 DDD Supple Design
notes.back: Make post-conditions and invariants explicit (in code or tests) so clients know what an operation guarantees without reading its code.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::08 DDD Supple Design
notes.back: Cut the design along the domain's natural seams, so changes stay local instead of rippling across arbitrary boundaries.
notes.analogy: Like carving a chicken at the joints rather than hacking through bone.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::08 DDD Supple Design
notes.back: An operation whose return type equals its argument type (like integer addition), so operations combine without new dependencies. Common on Value Objects.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::08 DDD Supple Design
notes.back: A class with minimal dependencies can be understood in isolation, cutting the mental load of every change.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::08 DDD Supple Design
notes.back: Express rules as precise, executable descriptions of what (e.g. composed Specifications) rather than step-by-step procedures.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::09 DDD Bounded Contexts & Context Maps
notes.back: An explicit boundary (subsystem, codebase, team) within which one model applies and each term has a single meaning.
notes.analogy: "Account" means one thing to the bank's ledger team and another to its login team; each gets its own context.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::09 DDD Bounded Contexts & Context Maps
notes.front: Why is one unified model for a large system a mistake?
notes.back: Teams fight over meanings and the model bloats into ambiguity. Split into Bounded Contexts and manage their relationships explicitly.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::09 DDD Bounded Contexts & Context Maps
notes.back: Frequently merging code and model changes within one Bounded Context, with automated tests, so the model doesn't splinter.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::09 DDD Bounded Contexts & Context Maps
notes.back: A map naming each Bounded Context and the relationships and translation points between them, giving everyone the global view.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::09 DDD Bounded Contexts & Context Maps
notes.back: Upstream's changes affect downstream, not the reverse. The power balance decides the pattern: Customer/Supplier, Conformist or ACL.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::09 DDD Bounded Contexts & Context Maps
notes.back: Two teams share a subset of the model and code. Less duplication, but every kernel change needs both teams to agree.
notes.analogy: A shared kitchen between two flatmates: less to buy, but every change to it needs both to agree.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::09 DDD Bounded Contexts & Context Maps
notes.back: Downstream (customer) needs enter the upstream (supplier) backlog; interface tests stop the supplier from breaking the customer.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::09 DDD Bounded Contexts & Context Maps
notes.back: A downstream with no leverage adopts the upstream model as-is. No translation cost, but it inherits upstream's flaws.
notes.analogy: A small supplier who just uses the big retailer's order forms as-is, quirks included.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::09 DDD Bounded Contexts & Context Maps
notes.back: A translation layer (facades, adapters) that keeps a foreign or legacy model from leaking into and corrupting your model.
notes.analogy: An interpreter at a border: each side keeps speaking its own language.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::09 DDD Bounded Contexts & Context Maps
notes.back: Conform when the upstream model is good enough and translation isn't worth it. Build an ACL when the upstream model would distort your core model.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::09 DDD Bounded Contexts & Context Maps
notes.back: Declare no integration between two contexts when integration costs more than it gains; each team goes its own way.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::09 DDD Bounded Contexts & Context Maps
notes.back: Expose a context through one formal, shared protocol/API for all consumers instead of a bespoke translator per consumer.
notes.analogy: A power socket standard: every appliance plugs into the same interface instead of custom wiring.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::09 DDD Bounded Contexts & Context Maps
notes.back: A well-documented shared language (e.g. a standard schema) used as the common medium between contexts, often paired with an Open Host Service.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.front: Core Domain: what is it and how do you treat it?
notes.back: The most valuable, differentiating part of the model, why the system exists. Put your best people and most refinement there.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.back: Separating the model's vital essence (Core Domain) from the supporting bulk, so effort goes where it differentiates.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.front: Generic Subdomain: how should you handle it?
notes.back: Necessary but not differentiating (time, ledgers, identity). Isolate it from the core; buy, reuse or outsource rather than craft.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.back: A short (≈1 page) description of the Core Domain and its value, written early to align the team on what matters most.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.back: Make the Core Domain visible (a distillation document, or flags in the code) so developers know what's central, without restructuring.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.back: A mechanism is a complex computation (the "how", e.g. a solver) factored behind a clean interface; a generic subdomain is a part of the model itself.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.back: Refactor so the Core Domain lives in its own modules, physically separated from supporting code, to strengthen its cohesion.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.back: Pull the most fundamental concepts and interactions into an abstract model, decoupled from specific implementations.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.front: What problem does a large-scale structure solve?
notes.back: Even with good contexts, a big system lacks an overall sense of where things belong; a system-wide set of rules/roles lets people navigate it.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.back: Let the large-scale structure grow with understanding, staying minimal; a rigid upfront structure fights the developers.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.back: Assign each part of the model to a layer of responsibility (e.g. Operations, Capability, Policy) that follows natural domain dependencies.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.back: A "model of the model": objects that describe and constrain the operational objects, so users can configure rules without code changes.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.back: Components interoperate through a shared set of abstract interfaces (an abstract core), so implementations can be swapped. Suits mature models.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.back: A shared analogy for how the whole system works (from XP). Use it only if it genuinely fits; a forced metaphor misleads.

notes.deck: Software Architecture & DDD::10 DDD Distillation & Large-Scale Structure
notes.text: DDD's three strategic tools: {{c1::Bounded Context}} keeps each model consistent, {{c2::Distillation}} focuses effort on the core, {{c3::Large-Scale Structure}} gives system-wide orientation.
